entries.caption: Does “her offspring” predict the virgin birth? Genesis never says this child has no human father. That interpretation comes from the later Gospel story.
Does Genesis predict Jesus defeating Satan? The serpent only becomes Satan in later Christian interpretation. Genesis itself describes conflict between humans and snakes.
Is Enoch’s disappearance a preview of Jesus’s ascension? Enoch avoids death; Jesus dies and rises first. The stories have a resemblance, but also a crucial difference.
Did Noah predict that God would join Shem’s family? He calls the LORD “the God of Shem.” Turning that into a prediction about Jesus adds far more than the verse says.
Did God’s promise to bless the nations through Abraham predict Jesus? Paul reads it that way, but Genesis speaks about Abraham and does not identify a future individual.
Does the singular word “offspring” identify Jesus? In Genesis, the same word describes descendants as numerous as the stars. Singular grammar does not make it one person.
Does Melchizedek’s priesthood predict Jesus? Genesis supplies a striking comparison, but the actual promise of a future priest appears later, in Psalm 110.
Do Melchizedek’s titles predict Jesus? “King of righteousness” and “king of peace” describe Melchizedek himself. Hebrews makes the comparison much later.
Does Melchizedek’s bread and wine predict the Last Supper? It is a natural Christian symbol—but Genesis calls it neither a sacrifice nor a prediction.
Does God’s promise to Isaac identify Jesus? Jesus belongs to Isaac’s family, but so do countless others. The passage promises a lineage, not one particular descendant.
Did Abraham predict Jesus as God’s lamb? The story answers its own question: God provides a ram for Isaac’s sacrifice. Connecting that ram with Jesus comes later.
Does Abraham’s “offspring” mean one future saviour? Genesis also compares that offspring to countless stars. Acts and Paul focus the promise on Jesus later.
Did God promise a rescuer through Isaac? Genesis promises Isaac land, descendants and worldwide blessing. It never identifies one future Messiah.
Is Jesus Jacob’s ladder? Jesus reuses the image of angels ascending and descending, but Jacob’s dream is about God protecting Jacob—not predicting another person.
Does Jacob’s family line predict Jesus? Jesus is one of Jacob’s many descendants. An ancestry shared with countless people cannot identify him by itself.
Did Genesis reveal when Jesus would come? The disputed word “Shiloh” and an undefined royal deadline cannot provide a clear date for the Messiah.
Was Jesus promised through Judah? The passage points towards rule from Judah, and Jesus has the right ancestry. But a large family line cannot identify one person.
Was the name “Shiloh” a title for Jesus? The Hebrew is difficult, “the one sent” is not a secure translation, and John never calls Jesus Shiloh.
Did Jesus have to arrive before Judah disappeared? Genesis speaks about royal rule, not the tribe losing its identity. The supposed deadline is not in the text.
Does one flock under Jesus fulfil the nations obeying Judah’s ruler? The images are similar, but John never connects them. Resemblance alone does not establish prediction.
When Jesus says “I am,” is he using God’s name? Perhaps—but Exodus reveals God’s identity to Moses. It does not predict a future saviour.
Does the spotless Passover animal predict Jesus? The comparison works as Christian symbolism, but an ordinary ritual rule shared by other sacrifices is not a unique prediction.
Does Passover blood predict salvation through Jesus? Both stories involve rescue, but Exodus describes protection from a plague—not forgiveness of sins.
Paul explicitly calls Jesus “our Passover lamb.” The Christian comparison is undeniable. But that does not mean the original Exodus story was predicting him.
John says Jesus’s unbroken bones fulfil Scripture. The match is exact—but Exodus gives instructions for preparing a Passover meal, not a prediction of the Messiah’s death.
Is Jesus’s name hidden in the Hebrew word for “salvation”? The words are related, but Exodus uses an ordinary noun. It is not naming a future person.
Does God’s holiness in Exodus predict Jesus? Christians believe Jesus shares God’s character, but this song praises God for a past rescue. It predicts nobody.
Paul says the rock in the wilderness “was Christ.” That is an explicit Christian rereading—but Exodus itself describes emergency water, not a future saviour.
Does God’s mercy in Exodus predict Jesus’s mercy? Both passages describe God being merciful. Sharing a quality is not the same as making a prediction.
Does the “pleasing aroma” of sacrifice predict Jesus? Leviticus uses the phrase for many repeated offerings. Ephesians later applies the familiar image to Jesus.
Did a healed man’s testimony lead priests to Jesus? Luke sends him to a priest, but Acts never links that event with its later priestly converts.
Hebrews explicitly compares Jesus with the Day of Atonement. It is strong Christian typology—but Leviticus gives ritual instructions, not a forecast.
Hebrews compares Jesus outside the city gate with sacrifices burned outside the camp. The connection is explicit, but it is typology rather than prediction.
Does “the life is in the blood” predict Jesus? It gives Christians a meaningful framework, but Leviticus states a broad ritual principle—not a unique forecast.
Leviticus says blood makes atonement; First John says Jesus’s blood cleanses sin. The later connection is real, but the earlier rule predicts no individual.
Jesus offers living water at the Feast of Tabernacles. The festival setting matters—but Leviticus’s drink offering was a different ritual, poured out to God.
John explicitly connects Jesus’s unbroken bones with Scripture. It is precise Passover typology, but Numbers originally gives a rule for preparing a meal.
Jesus himself compares his fate with Moses’s raised bronze snake. It is powerful Christian typology—but Numbers tells a past rescue, not a forecast.
Balaam’s future ruler has a serious messianic history. But “not now” gives no date, and the cited New Testament verses never connect Jesus with this oracle.
Is Jesus the prophet like Moses? The New Testament makes that case, but Deuteronomy’s context may promise a continuing line of prophets rather than one person.
When Jesus says Moses wrote about him, does he mean Deuteronomy’s prophet? It is plausible, but John never names the passage—and Deuteronomy’s meaning is disputed.
Did Moses predict that Jesus would speak the Father’s words? Jesus fits the description, but speaking God’s message is a prophet’s basic role—not a unique identifier.
Acts explicitly applies Moses’s warning to Jesus. But it also strengthens the wording from being held accountable to being cut off: a forceful Christian rereading.
Paul directly connects Deuteronomy’s curse with Jesus on the cross. It is powerful Christian typology—but the original burial law does not forecast Jesus.
Is Jesus the commander who met Joshua? The theological link is possible, but Hebrews never cites the story—and the apparent word match depends on English translation.
Is Boaz a preview of Jesus? His costly rescue makes meaningful Christian typology. But Ruth describes family property and marriage—not a forecast of Christ’s redemption.
Is Jesus the faithful priest promised after Eli’s family failed? Hebrews creates a plausible larger pattern, but Samuel’s story points historically to Zadok.
Did Hannah predict Jesus as God’s anointed king? Her song genuinely anticipates Israel’s monarchy—but “anointed” describes Saul and David too.
God promises David a ruling descendant; Matthew calls Jesus the son of David. It is a real dynastic link—but Solomon is the immediate promised heir.
Does David’s everlasting throne predict Jesus’s eternal kingdom? The wider Christian reading is plausible, but the temple-building son first points to Solomon.
Hebrews directly applies God’s father-son promise to Jesus. That is strong Christian evidence—but in Samuel, royal sonship first describes Solomon and David’s dynasty.
Did David’s everlasting house predict Jesus? The New Testament deliberately presents him as David’s lasting heir, though a dynastic promise cannot identify him alone.
Elijah’s ascent can meaningfully illustrate Jesus’s ascension. Luke may reuse the pattern—but Second Kings tells Elijah’s story, not a spoken forecast about Jesus.
Chronicles promises a ruling son of David; Matthew presents Jesus as Son of David. The wider link is plausible, but Solomon is the immediate temple-building heir.
Luke closely links Jesus with God’s Son, David’s throne and an endless kingdom. It is a strong Christian fulfilment claim, while Chronicles first points to Solomon.
Hebrews directly applies Chronicles’ father-son promise to Jesus. The link is strong—but it repeats the same Davidic promise already made in Samuel.
Job longs for someone to stand between him and God; First Timothy calls Jesus the mediator. The parallel is meaningful, but Job voices a wish—not a prediction.
Did Job predict bodily resurrection? Perhaps—but the Hebrew is famously difficult and may describe vindication before death. This claim is too uncertain for confidence.
Acts explicitly applies Psalm 2’s conspiring rulers to Herod, Pilate and Jesus’s opponents. It is a strong Christian reuse of an older royal psalm.
Jesus is called Messiah—God’s anointed ruler—and Psalm 2 became central to Christian claims about him. But “anointed” was a title shared by many people.
Does Psalm 2 predict Jesus’s holiness? No: “holy” describes Mount Zion, not the king. The claim attaches the adjective to the wrong noun.
Jesus fits the wider Christian reading of Psalm 2’s king. But the title “king” is shared by countless rulers and cannot identify him by itself.
The New Testament repeatedly applies Psalm 2’s royal sonship to Jesus. The link is explicit, though the psalm first described the reigning Davidic king.
Acts explicitly places Psalm 2 in its resurrection argument. But the psalm itself describes a living king’s installation—not crucifixion, burial or resurrection.
Revelation unmistakably gives Jesus Psalm 2’s iron sceptre. It is powerful Christian reuse, reshaping an ancient royal threat through Greek wording and the slain Lamb.
Psalm 2 blesses those who take refuge in God; John says belief in Jesus brings life. The trust theme fits, but John never identifies this verse as a prediction.
Jesus explicitly applies Psalm 8 to children praising him. The link is strong—but Matthew uses a present description of God’s glory, in its Greek form, for a new scene.
Hebrews makes Jesus the representative human who begins to fulfil Psalm 8’s calling. It is powerful theology, but the psalm itself mentions no Messiah or death.
Psalm 9 and Acts share striking language about judging the world justly. Acts may specify Jesus as God’s agent—but it never identifies the psalm as a prediction.
Acts twice applies Psalm 16 to Jesus’s resurrection and contrasts him with David’s grave. The argument is explicit, though the psalm alone reads as rescue from death.
